//: THE BACKUP POSTURE: what this project claims about its own recovery, and who holds the claim. WHY IT IS NOT LIKE ANY OTHER REGISTER HERE: every other control in this harness judges an artefact in the tree, and this one cannot — backups live in the platform's control plane, so the only way to learn their state is to ask over the network. That is why `node tools/check-backup-posture.mjs` rides a SCHEDULED lane and never `pnpm validate`: a check that resolves its answer from a live third-party endpoint reds an untouched commit on a morning nobody chose, which is the determinism rule that kept `pnpm audit` out of the chain. The JUDGEMENT is still proven offline — tools/lib/backup-posture.mjs is pure and unit-tested against recorded API responses on every `pnpm test` — because a credential-gated lane that skips everywhere has never been shown capable of going red. `maxDailyBackupAgeHours` SHIPS NULL AND MUST BE SET, and the null is the point: ASD's RB-01 asks for backups performed and retained "in accordance with business criticality", and business criticality is your determination, not this generator's. A number invented here would be an obligation with no framework behind it — the same error as inventing a patch SLA — so the harness supplies the mechanism and the requirement to decide, and you supply the number and the reason. It is only demanded once the lane is actually wired to a project; an unconfigured tree skips loudly instead. WHAT THE LANE ASSERTS: that SOME recovery mechanism exists — Point-in-Time Recovery enabled, OR at least one completed daily backup — and, only when PITR is off, that the newest daily backup is inside your tolerance. THE OR IS LOAD-BEARING AND IS NOT A JUDGEMENT CALL: the vendor states "If you enable PITR, we will no longer take Daily Backups", so an AND would red every correctly configured PITR project. AND FRESHNESS IS DELIBERATELY NOT ASSERTED UNDER PITR, for the same kind of reason: the vendor states that when the database has no activity no WAL files are backed up, and that the latest restore point may sit significantly behind the current time while still reflecting the current state — so a quiet, correct project would red on any recency bound. WHAT THE LANE CANNOT DO, stated here rather than discovered during an assessment: it cannot test a restore. Restoring is destructive to the target project, and the Management API has no clone-to-a-new-project endpoint, so restoration testing is a written, dated record below with a human's name on it — `documentation` tier, and labelled as such rather than borrowing the credibility of the checks around it.
why: REPLACE THIS, AND THE NULL ABOVE, WITH YOUR OWN DETERMINATION. Write how much data this system can afford to lose, and why — the recovery point objective your business criticality actually implies — then set maxDailyBackupAgeHours to the age past which a missing daily backup is a problem worth waking someone for. Two published facts to reason from: daily backups are taken once per day, so anything much past 24 hours means they have stopped rather than slipped; and Point-in-Time Recovery, where enabled, achieves a worst-case recovery point objective of two minutes, which is a different order of guarantee and is why enabling it replaces daily backups entirely.

restorationTesting.//: ASD RB-04 asks that restoration from backups be TESTED as part of disaster recovery exercises. Nothing in this repository can do that for you, and the reasons are structural rather than temporary — they are recorded here so the ceiling is visible before an assessor asks rather than after.
restorationTesting.whyThisIsNotAutomated: An in-place restore takes the project OFFLINE — 'The project is inaccessible during this process' — and the vendor publishes no downtime figure, only that it scales with database size. So a scheduled restore drill against production is an outage on a timer. (Note the careful wording: the vendor nowhere says a restore overwrites or destroys the existing database, so the argument here is availability, which is quoted, rather than destruction, which is not.) The non-destructive alternative is 'Restore to a New Project', and it is a DASHBOARD-ONLY flow: the published 115-path schema has no clone-to-project endpoint, an absence that means something because the same schema does publish nine `x-internal` operations, so unlisted is not merely hidden. Preview branches are NOT a substitute and NOT a counter-example either — the branching guide says branches start with no data from the main project, while the CLI's `--with-data` flag and the API's own CreateBranchBody.with_data say data can be cloned. That is a contradiction inside the vendor's own surfaces, so nothing here is graded on it in either direction. The `restore-point` endpoints are not a restore test either: they create a labelled rollback marker, both operations are marked `x-internal`, and the only way to exercise one is the `undo` endpoint, which reverts the same project. What remains is the honest drill: restore a `supabase db dump` into a scratch Postgres and confirm the application starts against it — bearing in mind the dump is not the platform's own artefact and omits the auth, storage and extension schemas. The evidence for that is a date, a method and a name, recorded here, read by a human, and never dressed up as a machine-checked control.
